summary:
AnalogTerraX is a web dashboard that finds Earth locations that resemble permanent Moon base sites and Mars landing sites. A user picks a world, a target site, and a mission activity: rover mobility, drilling, construction, EVA, instrument testing, or landing. The tool then ranks Earth candidate analogs on a map, with an overall score and separate topography, geology, and mineralogy scores.

Similarity comes from data, not from how a place looks. It compares slope and roughness from elevation models and laser altimetry (NASADEM, ICESat-2, LOLA, MOLA), rock types (Macrostrat), and minerals (EMIT). Each activity weighs these three aspects differently, and users can adjust the weights to re-rank the results.

Each site explains why it matches and where the analogy breaks down. A fixed note also reminds users that Earth can't reproduce reduced gravity, vacuum, or space radiation.

This matters because analog field tests reduce risk for Artemis and Mars missions. Picking test sites with evidence, rather than tradition alone, can turn up new and nearby locations, including in the Andes, and make mission rehearsal cheaper and more realistic.
details:
AnalogTerraX is a one-page mission-planning dashboard that finds Earth locations resembling permanent Moon base sites (Artemis south-pole candidates such as Shackleton and de Gerlache) and Mars sites. A user:

  1. Picks a world and a target site.
  2. Picks the activity to rehearse: rover mobility, drilling and sampling, regolith construction, EVA field operations, instrument testing, or landing and hazard assessment.
  3. Gets a ranked list of Earth candidate analogs on a world map, each with an overall score and separate topography, geology, and mineralogy scores.

How it works
A Python backend compares each target with Earth sites using measurable features only:

  • Topography: slope, roughness, and relief from elevation models and laser altimetry (NASADEM, ICESat-2 ATL03, LOLA, MOLA).
  • Geology: dominant rock type (Macrostrat).
  • Mineralogy: mineral groups such as iron oxides, clays, sulfates, and carbonates (NASA EMIT).

Each activity weighs the three aspects differently; landing depends on terrain, and drilling on minerals. Users can adjust the weights with sliders, and the ranking updates at once.

Opening a site shows:

  • a radar chart of the three scores;
  • "Similar in" and "Different in" points;
  • test ideas for the chosen activity;
  • a laser-altimetry elevation profile;
  • links to the data sources;
  • a fixed "Earth limits" note.

Benefits and impact

  • Analog field tests reduce risk and cost for Artemis and Mars missions, but sites are often chosen from tradition.
  • AnalogTerraX makes the choice evidence-based and transparent. Every match explains where the analogy fails, and every result is labelled a "candidate analog to evaluate", never an official one.
  • It can reveal new or more accessible sites, for example, in the Andes near our home city, Riobamba, Ecuador. That helps teams and countries without access to classic sites such as Antarctica or Devon Island.

Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: Next.js, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL, TanStack Query, Chart.js, and Zod, structured with clean architecture and MVVM.
  • Backend: Python with FastAPI. The frontend uses a typed client generated from the backend's OpenAPI spec.
  • Maps and imagery:
    • Esri satellite and OpenTopoMap basemaps.
    • NASA GIBS ASTER relief and macrostrat geology layers.
    • USGS planetary map services for Moon (LRO WAC, LOLA) and Mars (MDIM) site images.
  • Development and hosting: Docker, GitHub Actions CI, and Vercel.
  • Hardware: none.

What makes it creative

  • It reverses the usual question, from "What does this Earth site look like?" to "Which Earth sites behave like this exact Moon or Mars spot for this exact task?"
  • It tunes the ranking to the mission activity instead of using a single similarity score.
  • It says where each analogy breaks down, alongside why the site matches.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific honesty: the analysis covers only topography, geology, and mineralogy; a demo-data banner appears whenever results are placeholders, and the Earth limits note (gravity, vacuum, atmosphere, radiation) is always shown.
  • Accessibility: WCAG AA contrast, keyboard navigation, and reduced-motion support.
  • Clarity and pace: a guided first-visit dialog and a two-minute demo flow that fits the 48-hour hackathon.
  • Reliability: cached responses so the demo survives a flaky network.
  • Extensibility: New sites are backend data changes and need no UI code.
